item.title: Go Daily Question 223
item.description:
Consider the following 3 lines of code:

// 32-bit machine
1）var x int32 = 32.0
2）var y int = x
3）var z rune = x

Will they compile? Why?

If asked this question in an interview, you need to consider what the interviewer wants to test you on.

🔑 Answer Analysis:

Numeric Literals

In Go, literals are untyped. What does untyped mean? Untyped means they can be assigned to variables or constants of similar types. In the example above, 32.0 is an untyped floating-point literal, so it can be assigned to any numeric type variable (or constant). All of the following are legal:

item.title: Go Daily Question 214
item.description:
Below code output what?

func main() {
 a := [2]int{5, 6}
 b := [3]int{5, 6}
 if a == b {
 fmt.Println("equal")
 } else {
 fmt.Println("not equal")
 }
}
  • A. compilation error
  • B. equal
  • C. not equal
🔑 Answer Analysis:

Run online A. [2]int and [3]int are different types in Go and cannot be compared using the == operator.

./prog.go:8:10: invalid operation: a == b (mismatched types [2]int and [3]int)

item.title: Go Daily Question 119
item.description:
Consider the following 3 lines of code:

What is the output of the following code?

// On a 32-bit machine
1）var x int32 = 32.0
2）var y int = x
3）var z rune = x

Will they compile? Why?

If asked this question in an interview, you need to consider what the interviewer wants to test you on.

🔑 Answer Analysis:

Reference Answer and Analysis: Answer: Cannot compile.

  1. This is allowed because 32.0 is an untyped literal and can be assigned to int32.
  2. int occupies 32 bits on a 32-bit machine and 64 bits on a 64-bit machine. Although int in the problem occupies the same space as int32, they are different types and cannot be assigned directly, resulting in a compilation error.
  3. rune is an alias for int32, so it can compile.

item.title: Go Daily Question 092

item.title: Go Daily Question 049
item.description:
What is the output of the following code?

func main() { 
 var i interface{}
 if i == nil {
 fmt.Println("nil")
 return
 }
 fmt.Println("not nil")
}

A. nil B. not nil C. compilation error

🔑 Answer Analysis:

A For an interface type, the value is nil only when both its dynamic value and dynamic type are nil.

item.title: Go Daily Question 042
item.description:
What is the output of the following code?

func main() { 
 a := 5
 b := 8.1
 fmt.Println(a + b)
}

A.13.1 B.13 C.compilation error

🔑 Answer Analysis:

Reference Answer and Analysis: C. The type of a is int, and the type of b is float. Two numerical values of different types cannot be added, resulting in a compilation error.

item.title: Go Daily Question 031
item.description:
What does the following code print, and why?

package main

import (
 "fmt"
)

type People interface {
 Show()
}

type Student struct{}

func (stu *Student) Show() {

}

func live() People {
 var stu *Student
 return stu
}

func main() {
 if live() == nil {
 fmt.Println("AAAAAAA")
 } else {
 fmt.Println("BBBBBBB")
 }
}
🔑 Answer Analysis:

Output is BBBBBBB Simply put, an interface variable has two values: one is its type, and the other is its value. When checking an interface, the live() == nil condition is True only when both the value and the type are zero values.

item.title: Go Daily Question 029
item.description:
Which of the following assignments is correct?

A. var x = nil B. var x interface{} = nil C. var x string = nil D. var x error = nil

🔑 Answer Analysis:

BD. This question tests the knowledge of nil. nil can only be assigned to pointers.

A: Type not specified. B: Empty interface can be assigned nil. C: A string is essentially a read-only slice and cannot be assigned nil. D: error is essentially an interface type and can be assigned nil.
